extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and early-career television writers / new staff writers in TV writers' rooms
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for pitching ideas and participating verbally in a television writers' room, aimed at writers who are breaking into TV or have just joined a writing staff. Covers what a pitch is, room expectations, relevance, timing, and how to handle failed pitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a pitch (idea + presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pitch is both a noun and a verb: it's an idea ("Hey, I have a pitch!") and the presentation of an idea ("I pitched my sex dungeon idea yesterday and it completely bombed").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that 'pitch' refers to both the concept and the act of selling it; you may technically 'pitch a pitch' (but don't say that). Recognizing this dual meaning frames both what you prepare and how you present it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected participation
rubrics_metrics.description: You are expected to participate. That’s what you’re there for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being present is not enough — active verbal contribution is a core job requirement in a writers' room. Regular participation signals engagement and value to the staff and showrunner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal confidence and competence
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re an exceptional writer on the page but not great at speaking up, you must get over it and find the confidence to speak up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the skill of articulating ideas aloud; there’s no substitute for being able to present and discuss ideas in the room. Practice and pushing past discomfort are necessary to survive on a writing staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch to the showrunner’s direction / focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the showrunner will take the lead and describe in detail the specific areas she wants the writers to focus on that day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the showrunner specifies focus areas, tailor your pitches to those topics. At times direction will be looser, but when guidance is given, align your ideas to it rather than pursuing unrelated tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance: avoid wildly off-topic pitches
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most important aspects of pitching is making sure your pitch isn’t wildly off-topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to where the conversation currently lies; don't blurt out the first thing that pops into your head. Off-target pitches interrupt the flow and force others to redirect the discussion ('Oh, we already tabled that topic. Now we’re talking about this.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't pitch just to be heard
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t pitch simply to be heard. Just relax. Everyone knows you’re still in the room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contributions motivated purely by presence; low-quality or irrelevant pitches intended to remind everyone you exist are counterproductive and can derail the session.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and recover from pitches that bomb
rubrics_metrics.description: From time to time, no matter how hard you try, you’ll pitch something that bombs… You’ll want to crawl under the table. But it happens to everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalize failure: even experienced writers have ideas immediately turned down or met with silence ('the sound of crickets'). Shake it off, don’t let one bad pitch rattle your confidence, and move on to the next opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repeatedly pitching bad ideas ('stink bombs')
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t be that writer who’s firing off several stink bombs in a row.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple pitches are failing, pause and recalibrate rather than continuing to pitch poor-fit ideas. Repeated bad contributions damage your credibility in the room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen, recalibrate, and time your pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: If you feel a little lost in all the cross-talking and your pitches don't seem in sync, take a moment, listen closely to what story points or character traits are being debated, and mentally ease yourself back into the flow of the conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good timing matters: listen for cues, re-enter when your idea matches the current thread, and pitch when the timing is right. Even a slight nod from others is useful feedback that restores confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the informal, conversational nature of the room
rubrics_metrics.description: The pitching process is very informal and much more conversational than anything else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage expectations: not every pitch will be a home run and the process is conversational brainstorming rather than formal presentations. Repeated practice in this environment increases ease and success over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of acceptable pitches (character-specific to general story directions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitches can range from a particular character to a general direction for story areas to explore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to pitch at multiple levels of specificity depending on the prompt — from detailed character beats to high-level story arcs. Match the scope of your pitch to what the room is seeking that day.
